title: Layer-Wise Evaluation of Hierarchical Distributed Control for Hybrid Alternating-Current and Direct-Current Microgrid Clusters Under Packet Loss and Forecast Uncertainty
abstract: Hybrid alternating-current/direct-current (AC/DC) microgrid clusters require coordinated battery use, reliable restoration, and economic scheduling under communication and forecast disturbances. This study evaluates a three-layer distributed architecture in a constructed three-microgrid system using public load, solar, and price data from the California Independent System Operator (CAISO). The primary layer combines energy ratings and state of charge (SOC) for discharge sharing. The secondary layer models zero-order-hold (ZOH) receiver memory and tests mean-square stability under independent and identically distributed (IID) packet losses. The tertiary layer uses the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for distributed model predictive control (DMPC) with forecast correction and matched initial and terminal battery inventories across benchmark methods. On the selected stress day, compared with a grid-only baseline, operating cost and peak grid import decrease by 11.65% and 3.30%, respectively, while imported energy increases by 1.31%. The realized-cost difference from the centralized reference is 0.0029%. Supplementary tests examine longer discharge periods, complete communication outages, and reduced-order cross-layer behavior. Persistent-load-step tests reveal a restoration limitation of the original secondary controller. An integral candidate restores the tested deviations under combined disturbances. These findings characterize layer-specific performance and limited cross-layer responses within tested models. Field readiness and seasonal generalization remain unverified.
title_zh: Layer-Wise Evaluation of Hierarchical Distributed Control for Hybrid Alternating-Current and Direct-Current Microgrid Clusters Under Packet Loss and Forecast Uncertainty

title: Modelling and Simulation of a State-of-Charge-Based Electric Vehicle Battery Management System with Android Monitoring
abstract: .Existing electric-vehicle battery-management studies often treat CCCV charging, cell balancing, and mobile monitoring separately; few provide a reproducible simulation framework that couples SoC/capacity-aware discharge allocation with real-time Android monitoring. This paper presents a MATLAB/Simulink BMS for a multi-cell lithium-ion pack integrating CCCV charging, passive cell balancing, and a responsibility-based discharge allocator. Each cell is represented by an OCV-Rint/Thevenin equivalent circuit; SoC is updated by coulomb counting, and hybrid pulse power characterization (HPPC) pulses are used to verify the OCV–SoC relationship. In discharge mode, load current is distributed among cell-level DC–DC converters using weights derived from each cell’s usable energy, , subject to Kirchhoff’s current law, current limits, and SoC limits; this addresses capacity differences that SoC-only allocation ignores. The model was compared with uniform discharge under identical initial SoC, 30 A load, and cutoff conditions. The proposed method extended discharge duration from below 1,000 s for uniform discharge to 4,507.93 s, with SoC equalization at 706.82 s, 2,147.73 s, and 2,315.91 s for initial SoCs of 30%, 50%, and 90%, i.e. at least a 351% increase in runtime under the stated fixed-load simulation. A Jetpack Compose Android app using MQTT and Room/SQLite provided real-time SoC, range, energy, and runtime monitoring. Limitations include fixed-load simulation, no thermal/aging model, and the need for cell-level power converters to realize independent cell currents; experimental validation is required
title_zh: Modelling and Simulation of a State-of-Charge-Based Electric Vehicle Battery Management System with Android Monitoring
